title: Kernel windowing: quantization execution constraints and latency/cost tradeoffs
body:
Goal
-----
Design a lightweight "kernel windowing" model for the quantized execution path that lets the runtime make fast routing decisions (kernel choice, batching window size, and KV-cache affinity) with explicit controls for latency vs cost. This doc captures constraints, heuristics, open questions, and an initial set of experiments.

Why "windowing"?
-----------------
We observed two recurring tensions with low-precision kernels: (1) some kernels have very high fixed setup/dispatch overhead but low per-token cost (good for long sequences), while others have tiny amortized overhead but worse per-token throughput; (2) KV cache layout and eviction interplay with kernel choice — switching kernels mid-session can force cache normalization or re-layout, which causes latency spikes. The windowing abstraction is a compact state carried per-request (or per-route) describing the expected execution horizon and preferred affinity. The scheduler uses that to pick a kernel and batching window.

Core concepts and fields (proposal)
----------------------------------
- window_horizon: short | medium | long  -- cost-sensitive bucket describing expected remaining tokens for this request.
- kernel_preference: prefer-low-latency | prefer-low-cost | balanced  -- explicit tradeoff hint from higher layers or derived from SLAs.
- kv_affinity_hint: strict | sticky | any  -- indicates whether KV cache must remain pinned to a particular format/shard.
- switch_penalty_estimate_ms: stringized number (runtime computed metric) describing estimated cost of switching kernels for this session.
- prewarm_required: boolean-as-string -- indicates if we should prewarm dequant buffers before first token.

Reasoning: keep the per-request state compact (few enums + one numeric estimate) so fast-path routing (in C++) can consult it without heap allocations.

Compatibility constraints for INT8 / AWQ / GPTQ / FP8 kernels
---------------------------------------------------------------
- Format stability: AWQ/GPTQ kernels may require per-layer reorder or bitpacking that is incompatible across kernel families. If kv_affinity_hint == strict, we must ensure the selected kernel has a compatible weight layout or trigger a conversion step (cost accounted in switch_penalty_estimate_ms).
- Dequant buffer lifetime: some kernels stream dequant buffers and can reuse them across tokens; others allocate ephemeral buffers per-block. prewarm_required should be true for kernels with expensive one-time allocations.
- RNG & determinism: FP8 kernels have different rounding behavior; for SHARED_ROUTES where determinism matters (A/B tests, evals) kernel_preference should include 'deterministic' and the scheduler must avoid mixing FP8 and integer kernels for the same route.

Scheduler heuristics (first-cut)
-------------------------------
1) Bootstrap: on first request, derive window_horizon from route metadata (model, prompt length, user-specified max_tokens) and kernel_preference from SLA/cost-profile.
2) Kernel selection: pick the kernel that minimizes estimated_total_ms = switch_penalty + steady_state_per_token_ms * expected_tokens + batch_wait_penalty. Where expected_tokens map: short=<=32, medium=33..256, long=>256.
3) Batching window: enforce an upper bound on batch-accumulate time derived from kernel latency target. For prefer-low-latency, batch_wait_penalty increases by 2x.
4) KV affinity enforcement: if kv_affinity_hint == strict, only consider kernels that can use the existing KV layout; otherwise favor candidates with lower estimated_total_ms.
5) Mid-session adjustments: after every N tokens (configurable, default 8), recompute window_horizon using updated remaining token estimate and recent per-token telemetry (p95_ms). Only allow kernel switches if gain > switch_penalty * 1.2.

KV cache interaction patterns and mitigations
--------------------------------------------
- Sticky layout: for long-horizon sessions we keep a "sticky" KV mapping and avoid kernel switches even if per-token cost differs slightly. This reduces re-layout churn.
- Shuffle-on-switch: if switch is required, we do a background conversion where possible (copying to new layout while continuing to serve from old) and then atomically flip; this is only allowed when switch_penalty is estimated to be below a threshold or when session completes soon.
- Partial compatibility layers: implement lightweight adapters that can serve a subset of layers with new kernel while leaving others in previous format to avoid full conversion. Experiment matrix below.

Telemetry signals we need (short list)
-------------------------------------
- kernel_setup_ms (per kernel per model)
- steady_token_ms (p50/p95)
- kv_convert_ms_per_layer
- last_switch_ts and switch_count per session
- cache_hit_rate_by_layout

These should be surfaced per-model and aggregated by instance type so the estimator for switch_penalty can be derived online and updated across deploys.

Decision log / tradeoffs considered
----------------------------------
- Option A: always favor single-kernel-per-session (simple, robust) — wins for determinism but loses cost for mixed workloads.
- Option B: aggressive per-block kernel switching (fine-grained) — best for cost but complex due to KV conversions and memory thrash.
- Chosen hybrid: allow switches only when horizon is medium or long and when expected savings exceed conversion cost by margin. For short-horizon requests, prefer low-latency kernel and never switch. Rationale: most user-facing interactive workloads are short, and conversion overhead is high relative to request length.

Open questions and experiments (proposed)
---------------------------------------
1) Partial-adapter feasibility: measure per-layer conversion cost (ms) for AWQ->INT8, GPTQ->INT8, FP8->INT8 on our common model family (llama-style 7B and 13B). Goal: per-layer cost < 1.5ms for partial adapters to be viable.
2) Window sizing sensitivity: run A/B where short/medium/long thresholds are varied to observe p50/p95 latency and cost per 1k tokens.
3) Sticky affinity vs dynamic: instrument metrics for sessions that were forced to stick and compare throughput degradation vs cost savings.
4) Prewarm strategies: benchmark prewarm_required true/false for kernels with high one-time setup; measure tail latency impact on first token.

Checklist for implementation (MVP)
--------------------------------
- [ ] Add compact window state to RequestContext struct (C++)
- [ ] Implement kernel selector that uses precomputed kernel profiles (setup_ms, steady_token_ms)
- [ ] Wire KV-affinity hint through model load and session creation
- [ ] Emit telemetry metrics listed above (team: observability)
- [ ] Implement switch guard with margin check and safe conversion path (best-effort background conversion)
- [ ] Add config flags to override defaults for experiments

Edge cases and safety notes
---------------------------
- Do not allow kernel switches for requests that set deterministic=true in the API.
- If conversion runs out of memory, abort conversion and fall back to single-kernel serving; ensure we surface a clear error in logs and metrics.
- Limit per-session switch_count to 1 by default to prevent oscillation; allow tuning per customer.

Appendix: quick pseudocode for selector (conceptual)
-----------------------------------------------------
// inputs: ctx (window_horizon, kernel_preference, kv_affinity_hint), model_profile, telemetry
// returns: selected_kernel
function select_kernel(ctx, model_profile, telemetry, expected_tokens) {
  candidates = model_profile.kernels.filter(compat_with(ctx.kv_affinity_hint))
  best = null
  best_score = INF
  for k in candidates:
    switch_penalty = ctx.current_kernel == k.name ? 0 : estimate_switch_penalty(ctx.current_kernel, k, telemetry)
    steady = k.steady_ms * expected_tokens
    batch_penalty = estimate_batch_wait(k, ctx.kernel_preference)
    score = switch_penalty + steady + batch_penalty
    if score < best_score: best = k; best_score = score
  return best
}

Notes to reviewers
------------------
- This is deliberately compact; follow-up PRD should expand session lifecycle hooks and SLO mappings.
- Interested in quick experiments around partial adapters and background conversion; those are the highest-risk but highest-reward items.
